title: Attention Cost & KV Cache
summary: Transformers spend memory and compute on attention. The KV cache is the dominant serving-memory cost during decode — system designers must treat it as a first-class resource.

sections.title: Why attention dominates the systems budget
paragraphs: Self-attention lets every token attend to every earlier token. Naively, that is quadratic in sequence length for compute and memory. Training can often afford full attention; autoregressive inference cannot casually ignore the growing key/value tensors.

During decode, each new token reuses prior keys and values. Systems cache them (the KV cache) so they are not recomputed. Cache size grows with batch × layers × heads × sequence × dtype — frequently the binding constraint on GPU memory before FLOPs are exhausted.
bullets: KV cache: stored keys/values per layer for prior tokens

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Paged attention (as in vLLM) treats KV blocks like virtual memory pages to reduce fragmentation. Prefix caching reuses KV for shared prompt prefixes across requests. Separating prefill and decode onto different pools can improve utilization when traffic mixes long prompts with long generations.

When estimating capacity, start from concurrent sequences × expected context × bytes per KV element × layers — then compare to HBM. Quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4) and speculative decoding change the cost curve but do not remove the need for this estimate.

keyTakeaways: KV cache is often the real capacity limit for LLM serving
Systems tricks (paging, prefix cache, prefill/decode split) exist to manage it
